before.prompt: Describe how to read the volume of water accurately in a measuring cylinder.
before.canonical_answer: Stand the cylinder upright on a level surface and read the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level with it.

after.prompt: Describe two corrections to a volume reading taken with a tilted cylinder while the observer looks down at the water surface.
after.canonical_answer: Stand the cylinder upright on a level surface and view the lower meniscus at eye level.

before.prompt: State which dataset supports a valid test of the effect of temperature on reaction time: A varies temperature while keeping hydrogen peroxide concentration and catalyst mass constant; B varies temperature and hydrogen peroxide concentration together.
before.canonical_answer: Dataset A: temperature is varied while the other stated factors are controlled.

after.prompt: State which dataset supports a valid test of the effect of temperature on reaction time: A varies temperature while keeping hydrogen peroxide concentration and catalyst mass constant; B varies temperature and hydrogen peroxide concentration together.
after.canonical_answer: Dataset A: temperature is varied while the other stated factors are controlled.

before.prompt: State what is meant by precision when repeated measurements are compared.
before.canonical_answer: Precision describes how closely the repeated measurements agree.

after.prompt: State whether repeated masses of 8.21, 8.20 and 8.21 g show high or low precision.
after.canonical_answer: High precision: the readings differ by only 0.01 g.

before.prompt: Describe the difference between random timing error and a constant balance zero error.
before.canonical_answer: Random timing error varies between repeats; a constant zero error shifts the balance results in the same direction.

after.prompt: Describe the error types in these observations: stopwatch readings scatter either side of a reference; an empty balance always reads +0.25 g.
after.canonical_answer: Timing scatter suggests random error; the fixed positive balance offset is systematic error.

before.prompt: Name the apparatus most suitable for delivering one accurate 25.0 cm³ portion of a solution.
before.canonical_answer: A 25.0 cm³ volumetric pipette, used with a pipette filler.

after.prompt: Name the appropriate delivery device from this inventory for a 25.0 cm³ aliquot requiring ±0.1 cm³: beaker ±5 cm³; cylinder ±1 cm³; 25.0 cm³ pipette ±0.03 cm³.
after.canonical_answer: The 25.0 cm³ pipette meets the required uncertainty.

before.prompt: Describe how filtration separates sand from a mixture of sand and salt solution.
before.canonical_answer: Pour the mixture through filter paper in a funnel; sand remains as residue and salt solution passes through as filtrate.

after.prompt: Describe two corrections to a learner who filters sand in salt solution, keeps the paper to recover the salt, and discards the liquid.
after.canonical_answer: Keep the filtrate because the salt remains dissolved; evaporate some water and cool the concentrated filtrate to obtain crystals.

before.prompt: Describe how to obtain crystals from a salt solution without heating it to complete dryness.
before.canonical_answer: Gently evaporate some water to concentrate the solution, then cool it so crystals form and separate the crystals from the remaining solution.

after.prompt: Describe how to recover crystals from a hot concentrated salt solution when a learner proposes boiling it completely dry and rinsing the solid with a large volume of hot water.
after.canonical_answer: Cool the concentrated solution to crystallise the salt; separate crystals and rinse with a small amount of cold water.

before.prompt: Describe how to position a sample spot and solvent when starting paper chromatography.
before.canonical_answer: Place a small dried spot on a pencil baseline and keep the baseline above the solvent surface.

after.prompt: Describe the corrections needed if a chromatography sample is below the solvent surface and the baseline is drawn in soluble ink.
after.canonical_answer: Raise the spotted baseline above the solvent and replace the ink line with pencil.

before.prompt: Describe how simple distillation recovers water from a salt solution.
before.canonical_answer: Heat the solution to vaporise water, then cool the vapour in a condenser and collect liquid water.

after.prompt: Describe why a salt solution heated beneath an inverted cold surface can yield liquid water on that surface while salt stays in the heated vessel.
after.canonical_answer: Water vaporises and then condenses on the cold surface; the non-volatile salt does not vaporise with it.

before.prompt: Describe the role of a fractionating column when separating two miscible liquids of different boiling points.
before.canonical_answer: It provides repeated condensation and vaporisation, enriching the rising vapour in the more volatile component.

after.prompt: Describe why a fractionating column gives better separation than a plain delivery tube for two miscible liquids with close boiling points.
after.canonical_answer: Repeated condensation and vaporisation enrich the rising vapour in the more volatile liquid, improving separation.

before.prompt: Outline how colourless components can be located after a paper chromatogram has been developed.
before.canonical_answer: Mark the solvent front, then apply a suitable locating treatment to reveal the separated spots.

after.prompt: Outline the next two actions if a developed chromatogram has no visible spots and its solvent front is still wet. The sample may contain colourless solutes.
after.canonical_answer: Mark the solvent front before it disappears, then apply a suitable locating treatment to reveal colourless components.

before.prompt: Describe the separation and arrangement of particles in a crystalline solid.
before.canonical_answer: The particles are close together in a regular arrangement.

after.prompt: Describe which particle model fits a crystalline solid and why: X has widely separated moving particles; Y has closely packed particles in a repeating arrangement that vibrate at fixed sites.
after.canonical_answer: Y fits because it has a regular close arrangement and fixed mean particle positions.

before.prompt: Describe two differences between evaporation and boiling.
before.canonical_answer: Evaporation occurs at the surface and over a range of temperatures; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling temperature for the prevailing pressure.

after.prompt: Describe the phase-change processes in two records: A loses liquid only at its surface at 25 °C; B forms vapour bubbles throughout at its constant boiling temperature.
after.canonical_answer: A is evaporation; B is boiling.

before.prompt: Describe the observation and the particles actually seen in a smoke-cell demonstration of Brownian motion.
before.canonical_answer: Tiny smoke particles move irregularly in changing directions. The visible particles are smoke, not individual air molecules.

after.prompt: Describe which objects are visible and the cause of their movement in this observation: tiny smoke specks jiggle irregularly under a microscope; the surrounding gas molecules are too small to resolve.
after.canonical_answer: The visible objects are smoke particles, moved by uneven impacts from invisible moving gas molecules.

before.prompt: Describe how gas diffusion rate changes when temperature increases and when molecular mass increases, with other relevant conditions unchanged.
before.canonical_answer: Higher temperature increases diffusion rate. Greater molecular mass reduces diffusion rate at the same temperature.

after.prompt: Describe both trends in this supplied diffusion table: gas X travels 12 cm in 30 s at 20 °C and 18 cm at 40 °C; at 20 °C lighter gas Y travels 20 cm in 30 s under matched conditions.
after.canonical_answer: X spreads faster at the higher temperature; the lighter Y spreads faster than X at the same temperature.

before.prompt: Outline the changes to atomic structure introduced by Thomson and Chadwick.
before.canonical_answer: Thomson introduced negatively charged electrons within the atom; Chadwick established neutral neutrons in the nucleus.

after.prompt: Outline which later discovery contradicts each model: A contains only a diffuse positive body with embedded electrons; B has a nucleus but assigns all its mass to protons. Supplied evidence: positive charge is concentrated; nuclei also contain neutral massive particles.
after.canonical_answer: Concentrated positive charge contradicts A; neutron evidence contradicts B’s proton-only mass account.

before.prompt: Describe the electron-shell arrangement of a neutral calcium atom with proton number 20.
before.canonical_answer: 2,8,8,2: four occupied shells with two electrons in the outer shell.

after.prompt: Describe the completed shell arrangement of a neutral atom with 20 protons if its first three shells contain 2, 8 and 8 electrons, and identify its period.
after.canonical_answer: Two electrons remain for a fourth shell: 2,8,8,2; period 4.

before.prompt: Outline what happens during radioactive decay.
before.canonical_answer: An unstable nucleus emits radiation and changes towards a more stable nuclear arrangement.

after.prompt: Outline what these observations show about decay: a sealed isotope source continues to emit radiation when cooled, and its nuclei change from unstable X to more stable Y while the sample remains sealed.
after.canonical_answer: The emission comes from nuclear change, not escape of whole atoms; cooling does not stop this observed decay.

before.prompt: Describe the links between a main-group atom’s electron arrangement and its group and period, using Groups I–VII.
before.canonical_answer: The outer-electron count gives the group number; the occupied-shell count gives the period number.

after.prompt: Describe the group and period of a neutral main-group atom with arrangement 2,8,7, using Groups I–VII.
after.canonical_answer: Group VII from seven outer electrons; period 3 from three occupied shells.

before.prompt: Describe the changes in outer-electron count and metallic character across Period 3 from sodium to argon.
before.canonical_answer: Outer-electron count rises from one to eight, while metallic character decreases.

after.prompt: Describe both trends in this supplied Period 3 sequence: Na 2,8,1; Mg 2,8,2; Al 2,8,3 are metals, whereas P 2,8,5; S 2,8,6; Cl 2,8,7 are non-metals.
after.canonical_answer: Outer-electron count rises across the sequence; the listed elements change from metallic to non-metallic.

before.prompt: Describe the shared and differing features of the arrangements 2,1 and 2,8,1.
before.canonical_answer: Both have one outer electron; the first has two occupied shells and the second has three.

after.prompt: Describe one chemical similarity and one period difference predicted for atoms X 2,1 and Y 2,8,1.
after.canonical_answer: Both tend to lose one outer electron and form +1 ions; X is period 2 and Y period 3.

before.prompt: Describe the flame-test colours for lithium and potassium compounds.
before.canonical_answer: Lithium gives crimson red; potassium gives lilac.

after.prompt: Describe the identities supported by two flame observations using the supplied references: lithium crimson, potassium lilac, sodium yellow. Sample A is lilac and sample B crimson; clean-wire blanks show no colour.
after.canonical_answer: A supports potassium; B supports lithium.

before.prompt: Describe two typical properties that distinguish transition metals from Group I metals.
before.canonical_answer: Transition metals generally have higher densities and higher melting points.

after.prompt: Describe which sample better fits a transition metal using these supplied properties: A has density 0.9 g/cm³, melts at 65 °C and forms colourless salts; B has density 8.0 g/cm³, melts above 1000 °C and forms coloured salts.
after.canonical_answer: B better fits transition-metal properties through its high density/melting point and coloured compounds.

before.prompt: Describe the ordinary chemical behaviour and particle form of neon.
before.canonical_answer: It is very unreactive and exists as individual atoms.

after.prompt: Describe what is wrong with a model of neon showing paired Ne2 particles that readily lose one electron, given neutral neon’s shell arrangement 2,8.
after.canonical_answer: Its complete shell supports low reactivity, and ordinary neon should be shown as separate atoms rather than Ne2 molecules.

before.prompt: Describe the role of argon in a filament lamp.
before.canonical_answer: It provides an unreactive atmosphere around the hot filament, reducing reaction of the filament with gases such as oxygen.

after.prompt: Describe the better lamp-filling gas and the reason from this test: a hot filament rapidly forms oxide in oxygen but shows no such reaction in argon under the same conditions.
after.canonical_answer: Argon is better because it provides an atmosphere that does not oxidise the hot filament in this comparison.

before.prompt: Describe the compositions of brass and steel.
before.canonical_answer: Brass contains copper and zinc; steel contains iron and carbon, with other elements possible.

after.prompt: Describe the alloy names supported by these composition records: P contains copper and zinc; Q contains iron and a controlled small percentage of carbon. Reference key: brass is a copper–zinc alloy; steel is an iron–carbon alloy.
after.canonical_answer: P is brass; Q is steel.

before.prompt: Describe the electron transfer when sodium reacts with chlorine.
before.canonical_answer: Sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺; chlorine gains that electron to form Cl⁻.

after.prompt: Describe the ions formed when atom X with arrangement 2,8,1 transfers its outer electron to atom Y with arrangement 2,8,7.
after.canonical_answer: X becomes X⁺ with 2,8; Y becomes Y⁻ with 2,8,8.

before.prompt: Explain what holds positive and negative ions together in an ionic compound.
before.canonical_answer: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

after.prompt: Explain why an ionic solid resists separating into individual ions.
after.canonical_answer: Separating oppositely charged ions requires overcoming their electrostatic attraction.

before.prompt: Describe the arrangement of ions in solid sodium chloride.
before.canonical_answer: A regular repeating lattice of alternating positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions, extending in three dimensions.

after.prompt: Describe the correction to a sodium-chloride lattice model that places only Na⁺ nearest neighbours around one central Na⁺.
after.canonical_answer: The nearest neighbours should be oppositely charged Cl⁻ ions in a repeating three-dimensional ionic arrangement.

before.prompt: Describe the electron arrangement in a single covalent bond.
before.canonical_answer: Two atoms share one pair of outer-shell electrons.

after.prompt: Describe the electron count and bond error in an H2 sketch that places two shared pairs between its two hydrogen atoms.
after.canonical_answer: Hydrogen needs two shell electrons, not four; only one shared pair should join the atoms.

before.prompt: Explain the electrostatic attraction responsible for a covalent bond.
before.canonical_answer: The positive nuclei of the bonded atoms attract their shared negative electrons.

after.prompt: Explain why shared electrons can hold two positive nuclei together even though the nuclei repel one another.
after.canonical_answer: Each nucleus attracts the shared negative electrons; this attraction binds the atoms despite nucleus–nucleus repulsion.

before.prompt: Draw the Couper displayed formula for water, showing every bond.
before.canonical_answer: H–O–H, with one single bond from O to each H.

after.prompt: Draw the corrected displayed formula if a proposed water diagram is H–H–O, given that H forms one bond and O forms two.
after.canonical_answer: H–O–H, with oxygen central and two single O–H bonds.

before.prompt: Draw the molecular shape of water, H2O, with all atoms labelled.
before.canonical_answer: an O atom at the vertex of two angled O–H bonds.

after.prompt: Draw a corrected water model from this comparison. The supplied model places O between two H atoms on a straight line; the reference model has two angled O–H bonds.
after.canonical_answer: O at the vertex of a bent H–O–H arrangement.

before.prompt: Draw the molecular shape of methane, CH4, with all atoms labelled.
before.canonical_answer: a central C with four H atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement.

after.prompt: Draw a corrected methane model from this comparison. The supplied model puts all four H atoms in one plane around C; the reference model places them towards the four corners of a tetrahedron.
after.canonical_answer: Central C with four H positions in a tetrahedral arrangement, using wedge/dash or an equivalent clear 3D convention.

before.prompt: Draw the molecular shape of ammonia, NH3, with all atoms labelled.
before.canonical_answer: a nitrogen above a triangular base of three H atoms.

after.prompt: Draw a corrected ammonia model from this comparison. The supplied model places N in the same plane as a triangle of H atoms; the reference model has N above that triangle.
after.canonical_answer: A pyramidal arrangement, with N above the plane of three H atoms.

before.prompt: Draw the molecular shape of carbon dioxide, CO2, with all atoms labelled.
before.canonical_answer: O=C=O on one straight line.

after.prompt: Draw a corrected carbon dioxide model from this comparison. The supplied model bends O–C–O at the central C; the reference model has all three atoms on one straight line.
after.canonical_answer: Linear O–C–O.

before.prompt: Describe the bonding arrangements around carbon atoms in diamond and graphite.
before.canonical_answer: Diamond has four bonds per carbon in a three-dimensional network; graphite has three per carbon in layers.

after.prompt: Describe which carbon model fits diamond and the model that fits graphite: A has each carbon joined to four neighbours in a 3D network; B has three neighbours in flat sheets. Reference key: diamond has a four-bond 3D network; graphite has three-bond sheets.
after.canonical_answer: A fits diamond and B fits graphite.

before.prompt: Describe the local bonding arrangement in giant covalent silicon dioxide.
before.canonical_answer: Each silicon bonds to four oxygens, and each oxygen bonds to two silicons.

after.prompt: Describe why a model can have four oxygen neighbours around each Si yet the overall formula is SiO2, if each oxygen bridges two silicon atoms.
after.canonical_answer: Each of the four oxygen neighbours is shared between two Si centres, so there are two oxygens per silicon overall.

before.prompt: Describe two physical properties shared by diamond and silicon dioxide.
before.canonical_answer: Both are hard and have high melting points.

after.prompt: Describe which sample better fits silicon dioxide: X is hard, has a high melting point and does not conduct when solid; Y is soft and melts at a low temperature. Link the choice to structure.
after.canonical_answer: X better fits the strong continuous covalent network of silicon dioxide.

before.prompt: Describe the attraction that holds a metal together.
before.canonical_answer: Electrostatic attraction acts between the positive metal ions and the negative delocalised electrons.

after.prompt: Describe why a metal can stay bonded when layers of its ions slide rather than separating into individual atoms.
after.canonical_answer: Delocalised electrons remain among the positive ions; electrostatic attraction is maintained as the arrangement shifts.

before.prompt: Sketch a simple metallic structure using positive ions and delocalised electrons, with a key.
before.canonical_answer: A regular array of positive metal ions with small electron symbols distributed between them; key labels both and identifies electrons as delocalised.

after.prompt: Sketch the corrected metallic model if the proposed drawing contains neutral atoms with electrons fixed to individual atoms. Show the particles that permit conduction.
after.canonical_answer: Show a regular array of positive metal ions with delocalised electrons between them.

before.prompt: Identify the bonding types present in the constituents of concrete.
before.canonical_answer: Both ionic and covalent bonding.

after.prompt: Identify the bonding types present in the constituents of concrete.
after.canonical_answer: Both ionic and covalent bonding.

before.prompt: Describe two uses of different building materials: one for glass and one for metal.
before.canonical_answer: Glass is used in windows; metal can be used for roofing sheets or structural reinforcement.

after.prompt: Describe why ordinary window glass suits a light-admitting pane while a ductile metal suits a bent load-bearing bracket.
after.canonical_answer: Glass transmits light; a ductile metal can be shaped without brittle fracture and support the bracket load.

before.prompt: Outline the generalised structure of a soap molecule using a labelled head-and-tail sketch.
before.canonical_answer: A hydrophilic head joined to a long hydrophobic tail: ○────, with ○ labelled water-attracting head and the line labelled water-repelling tail.

after.prompt: Outline why a soap molecule needs regions with different interactions rather than one uniform region to help remove grease with water.
after.canonical_answer: A hydrophobic region associates with grease while a hydrophilic region faces water, allowing grease droplets to disperse.

before.prompt: Outline the chemical preparation of soap from a vegetable oil.
before.canonical_answer: Heat the oil with an alkali to hydrolyse it, then separate and wash the soap produced.

after.prompt: Outline why a classroom soap preparation is incomplete if oil is merely stirred with cold water and the mixture is labelled pure soap.
after.canonical_answer: Water alone under these conditions does not carry out the required alkaline hydrolysis; even a reacted mixture needs separation and washing to remove excess alkali and other soluble material.

before.prompt: Describe an electrode and its connection in an electrolytic cell.
before.canonical_answer: A conducting solid contacting the electrolyte and connected to the external circuit.

after.prompt: Describe why an insulating plastic rod cannot replace a metal electrode in the external circuit of an electrolytic cell.
after.canonical_answer: The rod cannot carry electrons between the external wire and reaction boundary, so it breaks the required current path.

before.prompt: Describe the difference between charge transport in the wires and in the electrolyte of an electrolytic cell.
before.canonical_answer: Electrons carry charge in the external wires; mobile ions carry charge in the electrolyte.

after.prompt: Describe why electrons moving in a wire do not imply that free electrons carry current through an aqueous salt solution.
after.canonical_answer: The materials have different mobile charge carriers: electrons in metal and ions in solution. The ionic solution conducts by ion motion, not the metallic mechanism.

before.prompt: Describe an electrolyte and the condition needed for its ions to conduct.
before.canonical_answer: It conducts when molten or in solution through mobile ions, and is decomposed by the current.

after.prompt: Describe why simply containing ions is insufficient for a solid salt to act as a conducting electrolyte.
after.canonical_answer: The ions must move through the material; fixed lattice ions cannot carry current through the solid.

before.prompt: Describe the polarity and electron-transfer process at the anode of an electrolytic cell.
before.canonical_answer: It is positive and oxidation, or electron loss, occurs there.

after.prompt: Describe why negative chloride ions move towards the positive anode but become neutral chlorine there.
after.canonical_answer: Opposite charges attract chloride to the anode; electron loss removes the ionic negative charge as chlorine forms.

before.prompt: Describe the polarity and process at the cathode during electrolysis.
before.canonical_answer: The cathode is negative, and reduction by electron gain occurs there.

after.prompt: Describe why Cu²⁺ ions are attracted to a negative cathode and lose their ionic charge when deposited.
after.canonical_answer: Positive ions are attracted to the negative electrode; gaining two electrons forms neutral copper atoms.

before.prompt: Describe the electron transfer when Cu²⁺ ions deposit as copper at a cathode.
before.canonical_answer: Each Cu²⁺ ion gains two electrons to become a neutral copper atom: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.

after.prompt: Describe why depositing one mole of copper from Cu²⁺ requires twice as many moles of electrons.
after.canonical_answer: Each ion has charge 2+; two electrons neutralise that charge for every copper atom deposited.

before.prompt: Draw a labelled electrolytic cell containing aqueous CuSO4 and two carbon electrodes connected to a low-voltage DC supply. Show polarity but do not label products.
before.canonical_answer: Two separated carbon electrodes dip into aqueous CuSO4; wires connect them to a DC supply, with anode positive and cathode negative.

after.prompt: Draw corrections to an electrolytic-cell sketch in which the two carbon electrodes touch, both are connected to the negative terminal, and the solution is aqueous CuSO4.
after.canonical_answer: Separate the immersed electrodes and connect one to each terminal of the DC supply; label positive anode and negative cathode.

before.prompt: Describe the electrode processes in molten PbBr2 using reduction and oxidation half-equations.
before.canonical_answer: Cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb. Anode: 2Br⁻ → Br2 + 2e⁻.

after.prompt: Describe why electrons appear on opposite sides of the two half-equations for molten PbBr2 electrolysis.
after.canonical_answer: Lead ions gain electrons at the cathode, whereas bromide ions lose electrons at the anode; the two transfers have opposite directions.

before.prompt: Describe the products at each inert electrode during electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide.
before.canonical_answer: Lead forms at the negative cathode; bromine forms at the positive anode.

after.prompt: Describe why molten PbBr2 cannot produce hydrogen and oxygen by discharge of its constituent ions.
after.canonical_answer: The specified water-free melt contains lead and bromide ions; it contains no hydrogen or oxygen source for those proposed products.

before.prompt: Describe the products of electrolysing dilute sulfuric acid with inert electrodes.
before.canonical_answer: Hydrogen at the negative cathode and oxygen at the positive anode.

after.prompt: Describe why electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid can consume water while the acid still provides an ion-conducting solution.
after.canonical_answer: Ions allow charge transport in solution, while the overall electrode reactions decompose water into hydrogen and oxygen.

before.prompt: Describe the products at inert electrodes during electrolysis of concentrated hydrochloric acid.
before.canonical_answer: Hydrogen forms at the cathode and chlorine at the anode.

after.prompt: Describe why concentrated aqueous HCl can give hydrogen at one electrode and chlorine at the other.
after.canonical_answer: Positive hydrogen ions gain electrons at the cathode; chloride ions lose electrons at the anode under the stated concentrated conditions.

before.prompt: Describe the electron transfer forming chlorine at an inert anode in concentrated hydrochloric acid.
before.canonical_answer: Two chloride ions lose two electrons to form one Cl2 molecule: 2Cl⁻ → Cl2 + 2e⁻.

after.prompt: Describe why the balanced chloride oxidation equation requires two chloride ions for each chlorine molecule.
after.canonical_answer: Cl2 contains two chlorine atoms; each starting Cl⁻ must lose one electron, giving two electrons in total.

before.prompt: Describe the products at inert electrodes during electrolysis of concentrated aqueous NaCl.
before.canonical_answer: Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode.

after.prompt: Describe why concentrated aqueous NaCl can leave an increasingly alkaline solution during electrolysis with inert electrodes.
after.canonical_answer: Water reduction produces H2 and leaves hydroxide ions at the cathode; sodium ions remain in solution with increasing OH⁻.

before.prompt: Describe the position of an object and the required electrolyte when copper-electroplating it.
before.canonical_answer: The object is the cathode, and the electrolyte contains copper ions, such as aqueous CuSO4.

after.prompt: Describe why a copper-electroplating bath needs dissolved copper ions and why the object must receive electrons.
after.canonical_answer: The ions supply copper atoms; cathodic electron gain converts Cu²⁺ to metal on the object.

before.prompt: Explain the meaning of an exothermic reaction.
before.canonical_answer: It transfers energy from the reacting system to the surroundings.

after.prompt: Explain why an exothermic reaction can warm a surrounding water bath even when no heater is switched on.
after.canonical_answer: The reaction transfers energy out of its reacting system into the surrounding water.

before.prompt: Explain the meaning of an endothermic reaction.
before.canonical_answer: It takes in energy from the surroundings.

after.prompt: Explain why an endothermic reaction can cool its surroundings while proceeding.
after.canonical_answer: It absorbs energy from the surroundings, reducing their thermal energy.

before.prompt: Draw an exothermic energy profile labelled with reactants, products, forward activation energy and ΔH. Label both axes.
before.canonical_answer: Energy vertical and reaction progress horizontal; products below reactants, with a peak above both. Activation energy runs from reactant level to peak; ΔH runs down from reactant to product level.

after.prompt: Draw an energy profile from these illustrative levels: reactants 30, products 10, peak 80 kJ/mol. Label both axes, forward activation energy and ΔH.
after.canonical_answer: Products lie below reactants; Ea = 50 kJ/mol upwards from reactants to peak, ΔH = −20 kJ/mol from reactants to products.

before.prompt: Describe the energy transfers when bonds break and when bonds form.
before.canonical_answer: Breaking bonds takes in energy; forming bonds releases energy.

after.prompt: Describe why breaking reactant bonds alone cannot account for an exothermic reaction.
after.canonical_answer: Bond breaking requires energy; net release occurs only if forming product bonds releases more energy than was absorbed.

before.prompt: Describe how burning a hydrocarbon fuel transfers energy and name its complete-combustion products.
before.canonical_answer: Combustion releases thermal energy to surroundings; complete combustion forms carbon dioxide and water.

after.prompt: Describe why complete combustion of a hydrocarbon increases the mass of the collected products compared with the hydrocarbon alone.
after.canonical_answer: Oxygen from the surroundings is incorporated into carbon dioxide and water, so the products include that additional reactant mass.

before.prompt: Describe how uranium-235 can act as a source of useful energy.
before.canonical_answer: Controlled nuclear fission releases energy as heat, which can be used in electricity generation.

after.prompt: Describe why a nuclear power station can heat water without burning uranium in oxygen as its main energy-releasing process.
after.canonical_answer: Uranium fission releases energy through nuclear changes; that energy heats the water without requiring combustion as the source.

before.prompt: Describe the basic arrangement of a simple cell that produces electrical energy.
before.canonical_answer: Two suitable different electrodes contact an electrolyte and are joined through an external circuit; a chemical reaction supplies electrical energy.

after.prompt: Describe why a simple cell cannot sustain current through an external wire if the ionic path between its electrodes is interrupted.
after.canonical_answer: Both external electron flow and internal ionic charge transport are needed; interruption prevents a complete sustained circuit.

before.prompt: Describe the energy-direction difference between a simple generating cell and electrolysis.
before.canonical_answer: A simple cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy; electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a chemical change.

after.prompt: Describe the energy-transfer directions inferred from these records: device X runs a lamp while its chemicals react, without an external power supply; device Y produces new chemicals only while connected to a DC supply.
after.canonical_answer: X converts chemical energy to electrical output; Y uses electrical input to drive chemical change.

before.prompt: Describe two energy sources that generate electricity without fuel combustion at the point of generation.
before.canonical_answer: Solar cells use sunlight; wind turbines use moving air.

after.prompt: Describe why a wind turbine and a hydroelectric generator can produce electricity without fuel combustion at the generator.
after.canonical_answer: Moving air or water transfers kinetic energy to machinery that drives a generator; the energy input is motion, not a burning fuel.

before.prompt: Describe the reactants and products when a hydrogen fuel cell generates electricity.
before.canonical_answer: Hydrogen reacts with oxygen, producing water and electrical energy.

after.prompt: Describe why a hydrogen fuel cell needs a continuing supply of both hydrogen and oxygen rather than hydrogen alone.
after.canonical_answer: Both reactants participate in forming water; a continuing reaction and electron transfer require both supplies.

before.prompt: Explain the meaning of reaction rate.
before.canonical_answer: The change in amount of reactant or product per unit time.

after.prompt: Explain why two trials producing the same gas volume need not have the same average reaction rate.
after.canonical_answer: They may take different times; rate compares quantity change with elapsed time.

before.prompt: Describe a method for measuring the rate of gas production from carbonate reacting with excess acid.
before.canonical_answer: Collect gas in a freely moving gas syringe and record its volume at measured time intervals after mixing.

after.prompt: Describe why a final gas volume alone cannot establish reaction rate, even when the measuring cylinder is accurately calibrated.
after.canonical_answer: Rate is volume change per time; accurate final volume says nothing about how long collection took.

before.prompt: Describe the colour changes when hydrated copper(II) sulfate is gently heated and then the cooled anhydrous solid has water added.
before.canonical_answer: Blue hydrated solid becomes white on losing water; adding water restores blue.

after.prompt: Describe why blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate can return after the white anhydrous solid is cooled and water is added.
after.canonical_answer: Heating removed water of crystallisation; adding water allows hydration to reverse the earlier change.

before.prompt: Describe the conditions and behaviour of a reversible reaction at dynamic equilibrium.
before.canonical_answer: It is in a closed system under constant conditions, with equal continuing forward and reverse rates.

after.prompt: Describe why constant concentrations at dynamic equilibrium do not mean the particles have stopped reacting.
after.canonical_answer: Forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so gains and losses balance and concentrations remain constant.

before.prompt: Explain the difference between an alkali and a base.
before.canonical_answer: An alkali is a water-soluble base that gives OH⁻ ions in solution; bases also include insoluble proton acceptors.

after.prompt: Explain why an insoluble oxide that accepts protons can be called a base but not an alkali.
after.canonical_answer: Proton acceptance establishes basic behaviour, while absence of water solubility prevents classification as an alkali.

before.prompt: Describe how Universal Indicator is used to estimate whole-number pH.
before.canonical_answer: Add it to a small sample or use its paper, then compare the colour with the supplied pH chart and report a supported whole-number value.

after.prompt: Describe why Universal Indicator colours must be compared with the supplied chart rather than reported as exact decimal pH values.
after.canonical_answer: The chart relates colour to a range or approximate whole-number pH; visual matching lacks the resolution to justify arbitrary decimal precision.

before.prompt: Describe the products and gas test for magnesium reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid.
before.canonical_answer: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen form; a small hydrogen sample gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.

after.prompt: Describe why hydrogen from a magnesium–acid reaction is tested as a small separate sample rather than with a flame at the generating flask.
after.canonical_answer: Hydrogen mixed with air is flammable; ignition at the generator could spread into gas there, whereas a small separated sample limits the amount ignited.

before.prompt: Describe the products of hydrochloric acid reacting with sodium hydroxide solution.
before.canonical_answer: Sodium chloride and water form in neutralisation.

after.prompt: Describe why an acid–alkali neutralisation can produce water while leaving a conducting solution.
after.canonical_answer: H⁺ and OH⁻ combine to water; dissolved salt ions remain mobile and can carry current.

before.prompt: Describe the products of a metal carbonate reacting with a suitable dilute acid.
before.canonical_answer: A salt, water and carbon dioxide form.

after.prompt: Describe why an open acid–carbonate reaction vessel can lose mass even though atoms are conserved.
after.canonical_answer: Carbon dioxide leaves the weighed vessel; the escaped gas still contains the atoms missing from the measured contents.

before.prompt: Explain the difference between a strong and a weak acid in aqueous solution.
before.canonical_answer: A strong acid ionises completely; a weak acid ionises partially.

after.prompt: Explain why a weak acid can remain partly un-ionised while still conducting electricity.
after.canonical_answer: Partial ionisation supplies some mobile ions even though many acid molecules remain un-ionised.

before.prompt: Explain the difference between concentrated and dilute solutions of the same strong acid.
before.canonical_answer: The concentrated solution contains more dissolved acid, and hence more H⁺, per unit volume under comparable conditions.

after.prompt: Explain why dilution changes the concentration of a strong acid without turning it into a weak acid.
after.canonical_answer: Amount per volume decreases, but acid strength concerns extent of ionisation rather than that concentration.

before.prompt: Describe neutralisation of an acid by a metal hydroxide.
before.canonical_answer: The acid reacts with the base to form a salt and water.

after.prompt: Describe why adding a small amount of metal hydroxide can neutralise some acid without making the whole solution neutral.
after.canonical_answer: Some H⁺ is consumed by the base, but excess unreacted acid can remain.

before.prompt: Describe aqueous acid–alkali neutralisation using its ionic equation and reacting-ion ratio.
before.canonical_answer: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H2O, with hydrogen and hydroxide ions reacting in a 1:1 ratio.

after.prompt: Describe why equal amounts in moles of H⁺ and OH⁻ combine in aqueous neutralisation.
after.canonical_answer: One proton combines with one hydroxide ion to form one water molecule; this balances both atoms and charge.

before.prompt: Describe how titration can provide sodium chloride solution suitable for salt preparation.
before.canonical_answer: Find the reacting volumes of HCl and NaOH with a suitable indicator, then repeat those volumes without indicator.

after.prompt: Describe why a salt preparation can determine reacting volumes using indicator and then repeat the reaction without indicator.
after.canonical_answer: The first titration fixes the neutralising proportions; repeating these without indicator avoids contaminating the salt product with indicator.

before.prompt: Describe the products when a metal oxide or hydroxide reacts completely with a suitable acid.
before.canonical_answer: A salt and water form; the salt contains the metal ion and the acid-derived anion.

after.prompt: Describe why calcium oxide reacting with hydrochloric acid forms calcium chloride rather than sodium chloride.
after.canonical_answer: The base supplies calcium ions and the acid supplies chloride; there is no sodium source in the reactants.

before.prompt: Describe a test for the gas released when dilute acid reacts with a carbonate.
before.canonical_answer: Bubble it through limewater; carbon dioxide turns the limewater milky.

after.prompt: Describe why limewater becomes cloudy rather than the carbon dioxide itself turning white during the carbonate gas test.
after.canonical_answer: CO2 reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate, whose suspended solid scatters light.

before.prompt: Describe how to obtain crystals from a clear solution of a soluble salt without evaporating it completely dry.
before.canonical_answer: Gently concentrate the solution, then cool it to crystallise and collect the crystals.

after.prompt: Describe two improvements if a salt-crystal preparation is heated until no liquid remains and the recovered crystals are then washed with hot water.
after.canonical_answer: Stop after sufficient concentration and cool to crystallise; wash separated crystals with only a small amount of cold water.

before.prompt: State the general solubility pattern for metal hydroxides, including sodium, potassium and calcium hydroxides.
before.canonical_answer: Most are insoluble; sodium and potassium hydroxides are soluble, while calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble.

after.prompt: State the general solubility pattern for metal hydroxides, including sodium, potassium and calcium hydroxides.
after.canonical_answer: Most are insoluble; sodium and potassium hydroxides are soluble, while calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble.

before.prompt: State the solubility rule for carbonates and its familiar exceptions.
before.canonical_answer: Most carbonates are insoluble, except sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates.

after.prompt: State the solubility rule for carbonates and its familiar exceptions.
after.canonical_answer: Most carbonates are insoluble, except sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates.

before.prompt: State the main chloride solubility rule and the silver/lead exceptions.
before.canonical_answer: Most chlorides are soluble; silver chloride and lead(II) chloride are exceptions in cold water.

after.prompt: State the main chloride solubility rule and the silver/lead exceptions.
after.canonical_answer: Most chlorides are soluble; silver chloride and lead(II) chloride are exceptions in cold water.

before.prompt: State the main sulfate solubility rule and the barium, lead and calcium exceptions.
before.canonical_answer: Most sulfates are soluble; barium and lead(II) sulfates are insoluble and calcium sulfate is slightly soluble.

after.prompt: State the main sulfate solubility rule and the barium, lead and calcium exceptions.
after.canonical_answer: Most sulfates are soluble; barium and lead(II) sulfates are insoluble and calcium sulfate is slightly soluble.

before.prompt: Describe a test for ammonium ions in a small aqueous sample, including the confirming observation.
before.canonical_answer: Add aqueous NaOH and warm carefully; the evolved ammonia turns damp red litmus blue.

after.prompt: Describe two corrections to an ammonium test in which cold NaOH is added and dry red litmus is held in the alkaline liquid.
after.canonical_answer: Warm carefully and hold damp red litmus in the gas above the liquid, avoiding contact with liquid or spray.

before.prompt: Describe the NaOH test result for Al³⁺, including excess reagent.
before.canonical_answer: A white precipitate forms and dissolves in excess aqueous NaOH to give a colourless solution.

after.prompt: Describe how a record for a suspected Al³⁺ solution should be corrected: “white solution after a little NaOH; the precipitate disappeared in excess”.
after.canonical_answer: Record an initial white precipitate, followed by a colourless solution when the solid dissolves in excess.

before.prompt: Describe the observations when aqueous ammonia is added gradually and then in excess to Zn²⁺ solution.
before.canonical_answer: A white precipitate forms, then dissolves in excess ammonia to leave a colourless solution.

after.prompt: Describe the evidence that rejects Al³⁺ in this two-candidate test: Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ both give white precipitates with NaOH; only the Zn²⁺ precipitate dissolves in excess ammonia. X gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia.
after.canonical_answer: The excess-ammonia result matches Zn²⁺ and contradicts the stated Al³⁺ behaviour.

before.prompt: Describe the NaOH and aqueous-ammonia observations expected for Ca²⁺ on separate portions.
before.canonical_answer: NaOH gives a white precipitate insoluble in excess; ammonia gives no precipitate or a very slight white precipitate.

after.prompt: Describe which candidate fits X and why: supplied references say Ca²⁺ gives a white precipitate with NaOH but no or very slight precipitate with ammonia; Zn²⁺ gives a white precipitate with both. X follows the first pattern on separate portions.
after.canonical_answer: Ca²⁺ fits; the absence or near absence of an ammonia precipitate distinguishes it from Zn²⁺.

before.prompt: Describe the effect of adding aqueous ammonia gradually and then in excess to Cu²⁺ solution.
before.canonical_answer: A light-blue precipitate forms; it dissolves in excess ammonia to give a deep-blue solution.

after.prompt: Describe the change of physical state in this Cu²⁺ test record: a light-blue solid appears after a little ammonia; after excess ammonia, no solid remains and the liquid is deep blue.
after.canonical_answer: A light-blue precipitate forms first; it dissolves to give a deep-blue solution.

before.prompt: Describe the NaOH test for Fe²⁺, including excess reagent.
before.canonical_answer: A green precipitate forms and remains insoluble in excess NaOH.

after.prompt: Describe the supported identification and one limit: reference Fe²⁺ gives green precipitate and Fe³⁺ red-brown with NaOH, both insoluble in excess. A fresh sample gives green precipitate remaining in excess.
after.canonical_answer: Fe²⁺ is supported by the green colour. Insolubility alone cannot distinguish the two ions.

before.prompt: Describe the result of adding aqueous ammonia to Fe³⁺ solution and then adding excess.
before.canonical_answer: A red-brown precipitate forms and remains insoluble in excess ammonia.

after.prompt: Describe why a learner cannot identify Fe³⁺ solely from “precipitate remains in excess ammonia” if the candidate table shows this for both Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺. State the further observation needed; reference colours are green and red-brown respectively.
after.canonical_answer: The excess-reagent result is shared. Record the precipitate colour: red-brown supports Fe³⁺, green Fe²⁺.

before.prompt: Describe how to obtain a reliable lithium flame-test observation under supervision.
before.canonical_answer: Introduce a small sample on a clean wire into a non-luminous flame, checking for a red colour.

after.prompt: Describe how to investigate a suspected lithium sample when the cleaned wire produces a yellow flame before any sample is added.
after.canonical_answer: Reclean or replace the wire and check a colourless blank; repeat with the sample and look for its own flame colour.

before.prompt: Describe a method for checking a suspected potassium flame result after a wire gives a yellow blank.
before.canonical_answer: Clean the wire until the blank no longer gives yellow, then retest the sample for lilac.

after.prompt: Describe why a suspected potassium result cannot be accepted when the wire alone gives yellow, and the sequence needed before retesting.
after.canonical_answer: The blank proves contamination; clean or replace the wire and confirm a clean blank before adding the sample again.

before.prompt: Describe a supervised flame test supporting calcium-ion identification.
before.canonical_answer: Place a small sample on a clean wire in a non-luminous flame and look for brick-red.

after.prompt: Describe the conclusion and repeat needed if a calcium sample gives a brick-red flame but the same colour was seen with the wire before sampling.
after.canonical_answer: The blank means the colour cannot yet be attributed to the sample; clean or replace the wire, check the blank, and repeat.

before.prompt: Describe how a teacher-supervised flame test can support barium-ion identification.
before.canonical_answer: Introduce a small approved sample on a clean wire into a non-luminous flame and observe green.

after.prompt: Describe which observation supports barium in a sample: the clean-wire blank is colourless, sample P gives green and sample Q gives yellow. Supplied references: barium green, sodium yellow.
after.canonical_answer: P supports barium; the blank rules out colour already present on the wire, whereas Q fits sodium.

before.prompt: Describe a carbonate-ion test including confirmation of the gas.
before.canonical_answer: Add dilute acid; the evolved gas turns limewater milky.

after.prompt: Describe why bubbles alone cannot confirm carbonate, and the next test on the collected gas. A separate metal–acid reaction also gives bubbles.
after.canonical_answer: Effervescence does not identify the gas; pass a separate gas sample through limewater and look for milkiness.

before.prompt: Describe the chloride test with silver nitrate, including pretreatment.
before.canonical_answer: Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate; a white precipitate forms.

after.prompt: Describe why a chloride test must be repeated on a fresh sample if hydrochloric acid was used before silver nitrate. Specify the replacement acid.
after.canonical_answer: Hydrochloric acid adds chloride and could cause the white precipitate itself; repeat with dilute nitric acid.

before.prompt: Describe the bromide result after dilute nitric acid and aqueous silver nitrate, with a dilute-ammonia follow-up.
before.canonical_answer: A cream precipitate forms and remains insoluble in dilute ammonia.

after.prompt: Describe the identity supported by X and the role of a follow-up: reference chloride gives white precipitate soluble in dilute ammonia; bromide gives cream precipitate insoluble in dilute ammonia. X gives a cream precipitate that remains in dilute ammonia.
after.canonical_answer: Bromide is supported by both observations; the follow-up distinguishes it from the stated chloride reference.

before.prompt: Describe the test procedure and observation for iodide using silver nitrate.
before.canonical_answer: Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate; a yellow precipitate forms.

after.prompt: Describe a valid conclusion when acidified X gives a yellow precipitate with AgNO3, a reagent blank gives none, and the reference table lists chloride white, bromide cream and iodide yellow.
after.canonical_answer: Iodide is supported by the colour match; the negative blank makes reagent contamination less likely.

before.prompt: Describe the nitrate test using aluminium, including confirmation of the gas produced.
before.canonical_answer: Add aqueous NaOH and aluminium foil, warm carefully, and test for ammonia with damp red litmus turning blue.

after.prompt: Describe why ammonia after warming a sample with NaOH and aluminium cannot by itself prove nitrate, and give a comparison that addresses the ambiguity.
after.canonical_answer: Ammonium already in the sample can also release ammonia. Test a fresh portion with NaOH and warming but without aluminium.

before.prompt: Describe the sulfate-ion test using barium nitrate.
before.canonical_answer: Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate; a white precipitate forms.

after.prompt: Describe why a sulfate test is invalid if sulfuric acid is added before barium nitrate, and how to repeat it.
after.canonical_answer: The acid introduces sulfate; repeat on a fresh portion using dilute nitric acid before barium nitrate.

before.prompt: Describe how to avoid a false ammonia result when testing gas above warm alkaline liquid.
before.canonical_answer: Hold damp red litmus clear of the liquid and spray, then look for red changing to blue in the gas.

after.prompt: Describe how to investigate a litmus change seen only when droplets from a warm alkaline mixture hit the paper, but not when paper is held in the gas above it.
after.canonical_answer: Liquid contact can cause the change directly; repeat with damp paper in the gas while shielding it from spray.

before.prompt: Describe how to record a carbon dioxide test without confusing the gas with the precipitate.
before.canonical_answer: Bubble the gas through clear limewater and record a white precipitate making the liquid milky, not a white gas.

after.prompt: Describe the corrections to “white carbon dioxide gas formed” when the actual observation was a colourless gas entering clear limewater and making the liquid cloudy.
after.canonical_answer: The gas is colourless; the white appearance is a solid precipitate in the limewater.

before.prompt: Describe how a supplied teacher demonstration distinguishes chlorine from ammonia using damp red litmus.
before.canonical_answer: Chlorine bleaches the paper; ammonia turns it blue.

after.prompt: Describe which gases fit A and B using this supplied key: ammonia turns damp red litmus blue; chlorine bleaches damp litmus. A turns it blue, while B removes its colour.
after.canonical_answer: A fits ammonia and B fits chlorine.

before.prompt: Describe the correct teacher-supervised test on a separate small suspected hydrogen sample.
before.canonical_answer: Bring a lighted splint to the small sample and listen for a squeaky pop, keeping the bulk generating apparatus away from ignition.

after.prompt: Describe the errors in a proposed hydrogen test that puts a glowing splint into the gas-generating flask while gas is still being produced.
after.canonical_answer: Use a separately collected small sample and a lighted splint under teacher supervision; do not ignite the generating apparatus.

before.prompt: Describe the preparation and placement of the splint in a teacher-supervised oxygen test.
before.canonical_answer: Extinguish its flame while leaving a glowing tip, then introduce it into the small gas sample; renewed flame is positive.

after.prompt: Describe why an oxygen test must be repeated if the splint was still flaming when inserted and merely continued burning.
after.canonical_answer: The observation does not show relighting; blow out the flame to leave a glowing splint, then test a separate sample for renewed flame.

before.prompt: Draw a simple particle diagram for a pure metal and an alloy, with a key distinguishing the element types.
before.canonical_answer: Pure metal: a regular array of one atom type. Alloy: a metallic array containing at least two keyed element types.

after.prompt: Draw particle models for two supplied solid-metal samples: P contains only copper; Q contains copper and zinc mixed within the metallic structure. Include a key.
after.canonical_answer: P shows one atom type; Q shows two atom types mixed in a metallic array.

before.prompt: Draw a particle model showing how differently sized added atoms disturb regular layers in an alloy. Include a key.
before.canonical_answer: Show regular host-metal positions disturbed by a second keyed size of atom.

after.prompt: Draw a corrected alloy model if every row is shown identical despite a key saying that one atom in four is larger. Show at least one larger atom and its local effect.
after.canonical_answer: Insert larger atoms at the stated proportion in a suitable small array and distort neighbouring regular layers.

before.prompt: Describe the two reactions by which carbon monoxide is formed from coke and the incoming air in a blast furnace.
before.canonical_answer: Coke burns in oxygen to form carbon dioxide: C + O₂ → CO₂. Carbon dioxide then reacts with more hot coke to form carbon monoxide: CO₂ + C → 2CO.

after.prompt: Describe why coke can supply carbon monoxide even though its first reaction with incoming oxygen produces carbon dioxide.
after.canonical_answer: CO2 subsequently reacts with hot carbon to form CO; carbon is available in the hot coke bed.

before.prompt: Describe the different starting materials and energy/process features of basic oxygen steelmaking and an electric arc furnace.
before.canonical_answer: Basic oxygen steelmaking treats molten blast-furnace iron with oxygen; an electric arc furnace electrically melts scrap iron and steel.

after.prompt: Describe the suitable steelmaking route for each feed: plant X receives molten iron with excess carbon; plant Y receives sorted solid steel scrap and electrical power.
after.canonical_answer: X suits basic oxygen steelmaking to oxidise impurities; Y suits an electric arc furnace to melt scrap.

before.prompt: Describe the main chemical stages in extracting zinc from zinc blende by the thermal route.
before.canonical_answer: Roast ZnS in oxygen to form ZnO, then reduce the oxide with carbon and condense the zinc vapour.

after.prompt: Describe why a zinc-blende process that skips roasting and lets hot zinc vapour escape will not recover the intended metal efficiently.
after.canonical_answer: Roasting converts sulfide to oxide for the stated reduction route; the resulting zinc vapour must be cooled and condensed.

before.prompt: Describe the electrolyte and cathode process used to extract aluminium.
before.canonical_answer: Pure aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite; Al³⁺ ions gain three electrons each at the cathode to form aluminium.

after.prompt: Describe the corrections to an aluminium-extraction proposal using aqueous aluminium chloride and showing Al³⁺ losing electrons at the cathode.
after.canonical_answer: Use aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite; Al³⁺ gains three electrons at the cathode.

before.prompt: Describe how roasting and reduction differ in a broad copper-extraction account.
before.canonical_answer: Roasting treats sulfide material with oxygen; reduction removes oxygen from suitable copper oxide to form copper metal.

after.prompt: Describe the chemical roles in this supplied copper route: a sulfide is heated in air to an oxide, then oxygen is removed from the oxide to produce copper.
after.canonical_answer: The first stage is an oxidising roast; the second reduces the oxide to metal.

before.prompt: State two syllabus uses of zinc.
before.canonical_answer: Galvanising iron/steel and making brass.

after.prompt: State two syllabus uses of zinc.
after.canonical_answer: Galvanising iron/steel and making brass.

before.prompt: State two syllabus uses of tin.
before.canonical_answer: Tin-plating and making bronze.

after.prompt: State two syllabus uses of tin.
after.canonical_answer: Tin-plating and making bronze.

before.prompt: Name two uses of uranium identified in the syllabus.
before.canonical_answer: Nuclear power stations and nuclear weapons.

after.prompt: Name two uses of uranium identified in the syllabus.
after.canonical_answer: Nuclear power stations and nuclear weapons.

before.prompt: Describe the carbon-containing products of complete and incomplete combustion of methane.
before.canonical_answer: Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide; incomplete combustion can produce carbon monoxide or carbon particles.

after.prompt: Describe why restricting the oxygen supply can change methane combustion products without changing the elements originally present.
after.canonical_answer: Less oxygen permits incomplete oxidation to CO or carbon instead of CO2; only the bonding and oxygen amount in products change, not element identities.

before.prompt: Describe the changes when ethene reacts with hydrogen over a nickel catalyst.
before.canonical_answer: Hydrogen adds across C=C; the double bond becomes a single bond and ethane forms.

after.prompt: Describe why adding hydrogen across ethene’s double bond produces a saturated molecule.
after.canonical_answer: One part of the double bond is replaced by bonding to one extra H on each carbon; the carbon–carbon bond is then single with valency four maintained.

before.prompt: Describe how catalytic cracking produces smaller hydrocarbons.
before.canonical_answer: Vaporise a larger hydrocarbon and pass its vapour over a hot catalyst, breaking it into smaller molecules including alkenes.

after.prompt: Describe why simply cooling long-chain hydrocarbon vapour does not achieve cracking, and the change needed to obtain smaller molecules.
after.canonical_answer: Cooling condenses existing molecules; cracking needs chemical bond breaking, for example hot vapour passing over a suitable hot catalyst.

before.prompt: Describe the conditions needed to make ethanol from glucose by fermentation.
before.canonical_answer: Use yeast enzymes in a warm glucose solution with oxygen excluded.

after.prompt: Describe two corrections to a fermentation trial in which glucose and yeast are boiled in an open container with a constant air supply.
after.canonical_answer: Keep the mixture warm rather than boiling to preserve enzymes, and use anaerobic conditions with gas able to escape safely.

before.prompt: Describe the structural difference between ethanol and ethanoic acid.
before.canonical_answer: Ethanol has an alcohol OH group on CH2; ethanoic acid has a COOH group with a carbonyl bond on that carbon.

after.prompt: Describe why an OH group in ethanol does not give the same characteristic chemistry as the OH within a carboxyl group.
after.canonical_answer: In a carboxyl group the OH is connected to a carbonyl carbon; the complete functional group, not the isolated OH letters, determines the characteristic reactions.

before.prompt: Describe one laboratory method for converting ethanol into ethanoic acid.
before.canonical_answer: Warm ethanol with acidified potassium manganate(VII), an oxidising agent; the ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid.

after.prompt: Describe why ethanol mixed with an oxidising reagent and ethanol merely diluted with water can give different chemical products. The first mixture is gently warmed under teacher supervision.
after.canonical_answer: A suitable oxidising reagent can convert ethanol to ethanoic acid; dilution changes concentration without producing that oxidation.

before.prompt: Describe how ethyl ethanoate is formed.
before.canonical_answer: Warm ethanol with ethanoic acid using an acid catalyst; ethyl ethanoate and water form.

after.prompt: Describe the corrections to a proposed ethyl-ethanoate preparation that combines methanol with ethanoic acid and claims water is a reactant in ester formation.
after.canonical_answer: Replace methanol with ethanol; water is formed along with the ester during acid-catalysed esterification.

before.prompt: Describe two structural reasons why polymers can differ from one another.
before.canonical_answer: They can contain different repeating units and different linkages between those units.

after.prompt: Describe why two polymers can have different properties even if both are long chains.
after.canonical_answer: Their monomer-derived units and linkages may differ, changing molecular interactions and chain behaviour.

before.prompt: Describe the formation of poly(ethene) from ethene.
before.canonical_answer: Many ethene molecules join by addition polymerisation as their C=C bonds become single bonds in a long carbon chain.

after.prompt: Describe why an ethene polymer model cannot retain a C=C bond within every repeat while also adding continuation bonds to neighbouring repeats.
after.canonical_answer: Keeping the double bond and both continuation connections would give carbon too many bonds; addition polymerisation replaces C=C with single backbone bonding.

before.prompt: Draw a generic nylon repeating section using R and R′ for the carbon-containing portions.
before.canonical_answer: [–NH–R–NH–C(=O)–R′–C(=O)–]n, joined through the terminal NH and carbonyl groups to neighbouring units.

after.prompt: Draw a continuing chain by joining the supplied fragments –NH–R–NH– and –C(=O)–R′–C(=O)– alternately. Mark the new linkage type.
after.canonical_answer: …–NH–R–NH–C(=O)–R′–C(=O)–NH–R–NH–…; the links are amide links.

before.prompt: Draw a generic polyester repeating section using R and R′ for carbon-containing portions.

after.prompt: Draw a segment containing two ester links by connecting HO–R–OH between the supplied carbonyl-ended fragments …–C(=O)– and –C(=O)–…. Remove each hydroxyl hydrogen when connecting its oxygen to a carbonyl carbon.

before.prompt: Name the three main classes of food constituents studied in this organic section.
before.canonical_answer: Proteins, fats and carbohydrates.

after.prompt: Name the three main classes of food constituents studied in this organic section.
after.canonical_answer: Proteins, fats and carbohydrates.

before.prompt: Describe the hydrolysis of a protein and name the product class.
before.canonical_answer: Water breaks the amide links under suitable conditions, producing amino acids.

after.prompt: Describe why a protein solution is not evidence of complete hydrolysis, and the product observation that would support that claim.
after.canonical_answer: Dissolution need not break peptide bonds; evidence of amino-acid products would support hydrolysis.

before.prompt: Describe how a complex carbohydrate such as starch can be converted into simple sugars.
before.canonical_answer: Heat it with a suitable dilute acid so hydrolysis breaks the links between sugar units.

after.prompt: Describe why two starch trials may differ if one is mixed with cold water and the other heated with dilute acid.
after.canonical_answer: Cold water alone does not establish hydrolysis; heated dilute acid can break carbohydrate links and produce simple sugars.

before.prompt: Describe how chromatography can help identify products in a hydrolysed food sample.
before.canonical_answer: Separate sample and reference substances in the same solvent run, then compare their spot positions or Rf values.

after.prompt: Describe why a hydrolysate spot with Rf 0.40 cannot securely be matched to a reference with Rf 0.40 measured using another solvent, and give a better comparison.
after.canonical_answer: Rf depends on the separation conditions; run sample and reference together with the same solvent and paper.

before.prompt: Describe how washing soda softens hard water.
before.canonical_answer: It supplies carbonate ions, which precipitate dissolved calcium ions as calcium carbonate.

after.prompt: Describe why adding carbonate ions can soften calcium sulfate water even though boiling it does not.
after.canonical_answer: Carbonate precipitates dissolved Ca²⁺ as CaCO3; boiling alone does not remove this permanent-hardness source.

before.prompt: Suggest a treatment for calcium sulfate hardness when boiling has failed.
before.canonical_answer: Washing soda precipitation or ion exchange.

after.prompt: Suggest a treatment for calcium sulfate hardness when boiling has failed.
after.canonical_answer: Washing soda precipitation or ion exchange.

before.prompt: Describe how boiling temporarily hard water both softens it and forms scale.
before.canonical_answer: Hydrogen carbonate decomposes, removing calcium ions from solution as insoluble calcium carbonate that deposits as scale.

after.prompt: Describe why boiling a temporarily hard water sample can leave both less dissolved hardness and a solid deposit on the vessel.
after.canonical_answer: Heating produces insoluble calcium carbonate; removal of calcium from solution softens the water while the deposited solid forms scale.

before.prompt: Describe the distinct purposes of filtration and chlorination in water treatment.
before.canonical_answer: Filtration removes suspended particles; chlorination disinfects by acting on harmful microorganisms.

after.prompt: Describe why clear water leaving a sand filter may still need chlorination before supply.
after.canonical_answer: Filtration removes suspended solids but does not reliably eliminate all pathogens; chlorination disinfects the water.

before.prompt: Describe a laboratory preparation and test for carbon dioxide using a carbonate.
before.canonical_answer: Add dilute acid to a carbonate; pass the evolved gas through limewater, which turns milky.

after.prompt: Describe why a proposed CO2 preparation using dilute acid and a metal needs correction, and how to confirm gas from a carbonate replacement.
after.canonical_answer: A reactive metal may generate hydrogen, not CO2; use a carbonate and test the collected gas with limewater.

before.prompt: Describe how oxygen is obtained by fractional distillation of air.
before.canonical_answer: Remove water and CO2, liquefy the air, then separate oxygen using its different boiling temperature from nitrogen.

after.prompt: Describe why an air-liquefaction plant must remove water before cooling, and why ordinary filtration of warm air cannot separate oxygen from nitrogen.
after.canonical_answer: Water would freeze and block cold equipment; dissolved/mixed gases are not separated by an ordinary particle filter, so liquefaction and boiling-point separation are needed.

before.prompt: Describe why nitrogen is obtained before oxygen when liquid air is fractionally distilled.
before.canonical_answer: Nitrogen has the lower boiling temperature, so it vaporises more readily than oxygen.

after.prompt: Describe which component is more volatile using these data, and how that affects distillation: nitrogen boils at −196 °C and oxygen at −183 °C at the same pressure.
after.canonical_answer: Nitrogen has the lower boiling point and preferentially vaporises first.

before.prompt: Describe one commercial route for obtaining carbon dioxide.
before.canonical_answer: Recover it from a fermentation or suitable industrial gas stream, then purify and dry it before storage.

after.prompt: Describe why CO2 recovered from an industrial exhaust cannot be sent directly to a drinks plant merely because it turns limewater milky.
after.canonical_answer: The test supports CO2 identity but does not prove purity; contaminants must be removed and the recovered gas checked against the intended use.

before.prompt: State one biological source of methane.
before.canonical_answer: Oxygen-poor decomposition of vegetation or digestive processes in ruminant animals.

after.prompt: State one biological source of methane.
after.canonical_answer: Oxygen-poor decomposition of vegetation or digestive processes in ruminant animals.

before.prompt: Describe the difference between unburned hydrocarbon and carbon monoxide in exhaust.
before.canonical_answer: Unburned hydrocarbon is fuel that escaped full reaction; CO is a product of incomplete oxidation of carbon.

after.prompt: Describe why incomplete combustion can leave both unburned fuel and carbon monoxide in an exhaust.
after.canonical_answer: Some fuel fails to react at all while some carbon is only partly oxidised; these are different degrees of incomplete conversion.

before.prompt: Describe two conversions promoted by a suitable vehicle catalytic converter.
before.canonical_answer: CO is oxidised to CO2, and nitrogen oxides are reduced to N2.

after.prompt: Describe why a converter can reduce CO toxicity while still releasing carbon dioxide.
after.canonical_answer: Oxidation changes CO to less acutely toxic CO2, but preserves its carbon atoms in an emitted greenhouse gas.

before.prompt: Describe the manufacture of lime from limestone, including the equation.
before.canonical_answer: Heat limestone strongly: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2. The calcium oxide is lime.

after.prompt: Describe the evidence for CO2 loss in this heating record: 10.0 g pure CaCO3 leaves 5.6 g CaO in an open vessel; the solid was not spilled.
after.canonical_answer: The solid loses 4.4 g; CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 explains that mass as escaping carbon dioxide.

before.prompt: State one industrial use of calcium carbonate other than as decorative stone.
before.canonical_answer: In cement manufacture or as limestone in iron extraction.

after.prompt: State one industrial use of calcium carbonate other than as decorative stone.
after.canonical_answer: In cement manufacture or as limestone in iron extraction.

before.prompt: Describe how salt works obtain sodium chloride from seawater.
before.canonical_answer: Evaporate water in ponds to concentrate the solution and crystallise salt, then harvest and purify the crystals.

after.prompt: Describe why salt works can concentrate seawater by evaporation but cannot recover dissolved salt by ordinary filtration alone.
after.canonical_answer: Evaporation removes solvent until salt crystallises; dissolved ions pass through an ordinary filter.

before.prompt: Describe the essential conditions and catalyst for the Haber process.
before.canonical_answer: Approximately 450 °C and 200 atm with an iron catalyst, using nitrogen and hydrogen.

after.prompt: Describe why an iron catalyst allows faster ammonia production without making the equilibrium ammonia yield larger at a fixed temperature and pressure.
after.canonical_answer: It speeds both forward and reverse reactions; equilibrium is reached sooner without changing its composition.

before.prompt: State one industrial use of sulfur dioxide.
before.canonical_answer: Bleaching wood pulp or use as a food preservative.

after.prompt: State one industrial use of sulfur dioxide.
after.canonical_answer: Bleaching wood pulp or use as a food preservative.

before.prompt: Describe the essential conversion of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide in the Contact process.
before.canonical_answer: React purified SO2 with oxygen over V2O5 at about 450 °C and near-atmospheric pressure: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3.

after.prompt: Describe the error in a Contact-process proposal that writes SO2 + O2 → SO3 and claims the catalyst is consumed to make the extra oxygen in SO3.
after.canonical_answer: Balance as 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3; oxygen comes from O2 and the catalyst is regenerated.

before.prompt: State one use of sulfuric acid.
before.canonical_answer: Manufacturing fertilisers or detergents, or as lead–acid battery electrolyte.

after.prompt: State one use of sulfuric acid.
after.canonical_answer: Manufacturing fertilisers or detergents, or as lead–acid battery electrolyte.

before.prompt: Describe how to read and record an aqueous burette level reliably.
before.canonical_answer: Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level, then record the value with the burette unit and suitable precision.

after.prompt: Describe two corrections if a learner reads the top of a water meniscus from above and records every burette reading to the nearest whole cm³ despite 0.1 cm³ divisions.
after.canonical_answer: Read the lower meniscus at eye level and record precision appropriate to the divisions, typically to 0.05 cm³ by estimation.

before.prompt: Describe an arrangement to measure gas volume during an acid–carbonate reaction.
before.canonical_answer: Connect the reaction flask through a well-fitting bung and delivery tube to a freely moving graduated gas syringe.

after.prompt: Describe two faults in a gas-collection design: the reaction flask is open and its delivery tube ends outside a gas syringe.
after.canonical_answer: The flask needs a fitted bung and delivery connection; the tube must connect to a movable-plunger syringe so generated gas enters it.

before.prompt: Draw a labelled filtration arrangement for separating an insoluble solid from its liquid.
before.canonical_answer: A funnel lined with filter paper sits above a receiving vessel; solid residue stays on the paper and filtrate collects below.

after.prompt: Draw corrections to this filtration arrangement: paper lies flat across the beaker mouth, while a bare funnel containing the suspension stands beside it.
after.canonical_answer: Place folded filter paper inside the funnel above a receiving beaker; show residue retained on the paper and filtrate draining into the beaker.

before.prompt: Describe suitable apparatus for transferring exactly 25.0 cm³ solution to a titration flask and explain the choice.
before.canonical_answer: Use a 25.0 cm³ volumetric pipette with a pipette filler; it is designed for an accurate fixed-volume transfer.

after.prompt: Describe which apparatus meets this requirement and why: deliver 25.0 cm³ with uncertainty no greater than 0.1 cm³. Available devices are a 25.0 cm³ pipette ±0.03 cm³ and a cylinder ±0.5 cm³.
after.canonical_answer: The pipette meets the uncertainty requirement; the cylinder does not.

before.prompt: Describe two essential features of a graph of temperature against time from a cooling experiment.
before.canonical_answer: Label axes as time/min and temperature/°C with even suitable scales; plot the measured points accurately and draw a suitable cooling curve.

after.prompt: Describe corrections to a cooling graph whose time axis has equally spaced labels 0, 2, 8, 10 min and whose temperature axis has no unit.
after.canonical_answer: Use positions proportional to elapsed time and label temperature in °C.

before.prompt: Describe the test for carbon dioxide and its positive observation.
before.canonical_answer: Pass the gas through limewater; it becomes milky because a precipitate forms.

after.prompt: Describe why “the gas was white” is an incorrect conclusion when a colourless gas makes limewater milky, and identify the substance causing the milkiness.
after.canonical_answer: The white appearance is a precipitate in the limewater, not the gas; insoluble calcium carbonate causes it.
